name: Silicone scar sheets
lead: Silicone scar sheets are adhesive, reusable sheets of medical-grade silicone gel that are worn over a healed scar for much of the day over weeks to months. They are used mainly for raised hypertrophic scars and keloids and are sometimes applied after surgery or acne. Consumer packs are typically priced at about $10 to $30.

Silicone gel sheeting has been used in scar management for several decades, and a controlled trial published in 1989 reported its effects on hypertrophic scars [1]. An international panel of experts in 2002 identified silicone gel sheeting and intralesional corticosteroids as having a primary role in managing abnormal scars [2]. A 2010 review concluded that there was good evidence for silicone sheets, pulsed dye laser, intralesional triamcinolone and dermabrasion in reducing hypertrophic scars, with qualifications about timing and scar type [3]. Cochrane reviews of silicone gel sheeting, in contrast, describe the certainty of the evidence as limited because of the quality of trials [4][5]. Randomized trials have also reported results of no benefit in some settings, such as scar prevention in children with cancer [6].

paras: Silicone scar sheets are soft, flexible sheets that adhere to intact skin over a scar. They are distinct from silicone gel applied from a tube, which forms a thin flexible film over a scar; a 2008 review discussed both formats [7]. Sheets are typically cut to size, worn for a set number of hours per day, washed and reused.

Scars are areas of fibrous tissue that replace normal skin after injury. Hypertrophic scars are raised but stay within the wound boundaries, while keloids can extend beyond them and are most common in people with darker skin, according to Wikipedia [8].

Silicone gel sheeting is described as having been used successfully in scar management for more than 20 years as of a 2008 review [7]. A 1989 prospective controlled trial applied silicone gel sheeting for 8 weeks to 14 hypertrophic scars in 10 adults and compared them with untreated mirror-image or adjacent control scars using photography, biopsies and elastometry [1]. A 1994 randomized controlled trial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology assessed silicone gel sheeting in hypertrophic scars and keloids [9]. A 1995 study reported on use in evolving scars worn at least 12 hours per day in 20 cases [10]. A 2002 expert panel produced international recommendations on scar management [2].

The mechanism is not fully established. A hydration explanation has been proposed, in which occlusion increases hydration of the outer skin layer, and a 1996 trial of hydrocolloid dressing explicitly framed silicone's mechanism as related to scar hydration [11]. A 2008 review discussed the mechanism of action of silicone therapy in scar management [7]. A rabbit ear model has been used to study silicone gel sheeting in laboratory settings [12]. The first-pass site summary also proposes effects on fibroblast activity and collagen production through occlusion and gentle pressure.

Expert and review sources are generally favourable. The 2002 international panel highlighted silicone gel sheeting and intralesional corticosteroids as primary options [2]. A 2010 review in an otolaryngology journal stated there was good evidence for silicone sheets, with qualifications [3]. A 2024 review of pharmacotherapy for keloids and hypertrophic scars describes silicone gel and sheeting as sometimes used in combination with surgery, laser and other treatments [13].

Systematic reviews are more cautious. Cochrane reviews of silicone gel sheeting for hypertrophic and keloid scars, in 2013 and in an updated 2022 review for treating hypertrophic scars, assess the certainty of evidence as limited because of study quality [4][5][14]. Results vary by setting: a randomized trial in children with cancer reported no efficacy for preventing abnormal scars [6], while a randomized trial in a Chinese population with post-traumatic hypertrophic scars examined a silicone gel sheeting product [15].

Controlled and randomized studies include the 1989 controlled trial of 14 scars in 10 adults [1], a 1994 randomized controlled trial in hypertrophic scars and keloids [9], a 1999 single-blind randomized study comparing 585-nm pulsed dye laser and silicone gel sheeting [16], a 2006 randomized trial of silicone gel sheeting on post-traumatic hypertrophic scars in a Chinese population [15], and a 2015 randomized trial reporting no efficacy for prevention of abnormal scarring in children with cancer [6]. A 2001 report examined prophylactic use of silicone gel sheets after surgery in an office setting [17].

Reviews include Cochrane systematic reviews published in 2013 and 2022 [4][5][14] and a 2001 article on silicone gel sheeting in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery [18]. A 1996 randomized trial of hydrocolloid dressing versus moisturizer in keloids and hypertrophic scars examined a related occlusive approach [11].

Commonly described side effects are rash, itching and skin maceration, and hygiene of the sheet is a recognised consideration. Product guidance generally advises not applying sheets to open wounds. Reports from the controlled trials list skin reactions among adverse events, though details vary by study.

Scar sheets are discussed as an inexpensive step for raised facial scars, for example after acne or surgery. Forum material for this entry was not available, so this article does not characterise community opinion.
Products vary by sheet size, adhesive, whether sheets can be washed and reused, and recommended wear time, with listed prices of about $10 to $30.
